source_input: From the client's use-case list (Yusuf), item 8, Configuration Comparison Automation: "Planning automation and comparing configuration of 2 different platforms, may be cloud-cloud, physical to cloud or cloud to physical." The list closes with: "Our Aim is to do automation using Claude for all these content."
why_this_course: Load balancer migrations fail quietly. A configuration rebuilt on a new platform can look complete and still differ in a persistence timeout, a monitor interval or a pool's failover design, and the difference only shows up after cut-over. The client asked for automation that plans these migrations and compares configurations across platforms in all three directions: cloud to cloud, physical to cloud and cloud to physical.

Vendor tools help within one ecosystem. NetScaler can diff two ns.conf files [c2] and migrate applications with StyleBooks [c3], and F5 offers ACC and Journeys for AS3 and platform migrations [c6][c7]. None of them compares an F5 with a NetScaler, an ALB [c4] or an Application Gateway [c5], and the dialects differ in objects, defaults and units, for example F5's 180-second source-address persistence default [c18] versus NetScaler's lbvserver timeout default of 2 [c16].

The course teaches a pipeline that closes that gap without giving an agent write access to anything: read-only collectors, a canonical Pydantic model with provenance, a deterministic diff engine, and Claude used for planning and explanation through scoped tools and structured output [c8][c12][c13]. Results go through GitHub pull requests and ServiceNow changes [c26][c27], so every difference is verified, explained and approved before the change window opens.

design_decisions.decision: Treat 'planning automation' and 'comparing configuration' as two halves: a Claude planning agent and a deterministic diff engine.
design_decisions.rationale: The client input names both; planning benefits from language reasoning, while the comparison itself must be repeatable and testable.

design_decisions.decision: Normalize every platform into one canonical model before comparing.
design_decisions.rationale: Different dialects, defaults and units make raw diffs meaningless [c1][c2][c16][c18]; a canonical model makes all three directions use the same engine.

design_decisions.decision: Claude never computes the diff and has no write tools.
design_decisions.rationale: Determinism and safety: the engine is tested with seeded mismatches, and MCP guidance calls for human control over tool use [c14].

design_decisions.decision: Use F5 to NetScaler as the main physical-to-cloud scenario, with ALB and Application Gateway as cloud references and Terraform state for cloud-side resources.
design_decisions.rationale: F5 and NetScaler are the platforms named across the client's use cases; Terraform is how cloud load balancers are commonly defined [c9][c24].

design_decisions.decision: Include Radware Alteon, 'Anaya LB' and Cisco APIC collectors, using fixtures where lab access is not available.
design_decisions.rationale: The client's estate includes these platforms; recorded fixtures keep the lab affordable and reproducible [c22][c23].

design_decisions.decision: Gate results through GitHub pull requests and ServiceNow changes.
design_decisions.rationale: These are the client's existing review and change systems, and both have documented API and protection features [c26][c27][c31].

audience_profile.needs: Prove a migrated configuration matches before cut-over.
audience_profile.starting_point: Expert in one vendor's CLI, some Python, little cloud load balancer experience.

audience_profile.needs: Map appliance features to ALB, App Gateway or cloud NetScaler and detect drift from Terraform.
audience_profile.starting_point: Comfortable with Terraform and cloud consoles, less with appliance configuration.

audience_profile.needs: Readable drift summaries and remediation steps.
A governed, testable pattern for using Claude in change-related automation.

modules.title: Configuration comparison as a migration discipline
modules.goal: Learners define what a configuration comparison must prove for each migration direction and produce the object checklist the pipeline will automate.
learning_objectives: Learners can state what must be proven before cut-over for cloud-to-cloud, physical-to-cloud and cloud-to-physical moves.
Learners can explain why a text diff between vendor dialects is meaningless and what a semantic comparison compares instead.
Learners can scope a comparison by object type and list what cannot be compared.
Learners can describe the course pattern: Claude plans and explains, code computes, a person approves, everything is logged.

lessons.title: Three directions, three proofs
points: Physical to cloud: every VIP, pool, monitor, persistence and certificate on the appliance has a mapped target object or a documented gap.

Cloud to cloud: AWS ALB listeners, rules and target groups [c4] versus Azure Application Gateway listeners, routing rules, backend settings and pools [c5]; constructs differ even where intent is the same.
Cloud to physical: cloud defaults (for example ALB round robin [c4], App Gateway HTTP/1.1 to backends [c5]) must be made explicit on the appliance.
The deliverable for each direction is the same: a severity-classified difference report plus a list of things that cannot be compared.

lessons.title: Why text diff fails
points: BIG-IP describes a virtual server with destination, pool, profiles, persist, rules, policies and source-address-translation [c1]; NetScaler uses lbvserver, servicegroup, monitor and policy bindings in ns.conf [c2][c16].
Same-vendor diff tools exist (NetScaler diff ns config compares two ns.conf files [c2]; Alteon diff flash shows pending versus saved [c23]) but they only compare one dialect.
Defaults hide meaning: F5 source-address persistence defaults to 180 seconds [c18] while NetScaler's lbvserver timeout defaults to 2 [c16]; an omitted line on one side is not 'no difference'.
Units differ by platform; normalize before comparing.

lessons.title: Scoping the comparison
points: In scope: virtual servers, pools and members, monitors, persistence, SSL profiles and certificates, policies (iRules, LTM policies, responder or rewrite), routing and NAT.
Mark each object type comparable, comparable with mapping, or not comparable (for example iRule logic versus a responder policy is reviewed by a person).
Capture dependencies: monitors before pools, pools before virtual servers.
Record which runtime state is excluded (statistics, connection counts) because it is not configuration.

lessons.title: The course pattern
points: Claude plans, drafts and explains; deterministic Python collects, normalizes and diffs; a person approves; every prompt and tool call is logged.
MCP calls for a human in the loop who can deny tool invocations [c14]; the pipeline exposes no write tools to Claude at all.
The module 1 checklist is the acceptance standard for the capstone.
Each later module ends with a deliverable that slots into this pattern: collectors, model, plan, diff, explanation, approval, pipeline.

instructor_demo: Show a short bigip.conf virtual server stanza and the equivalent ns.conf lines side by side [c1][c2].
Run a plain text diff on them and show that every line differs.
Run diff ns config on two NetScaler files to show what a same-vendor diff can and cannot do [c2].
Point out the persistence default trap (180 seconds on F5 [c18], default 2 on NetScaler [c16]).
Build the first rows of the object checklist with the class.
Show the target capstone approval package so learners see the end state.

lab.brief: Take a sample physical F5 configuration and a hand-built cloud NetScaler configuration and write, by hand, the comparison plan and object checklist that the pipeline must later automate.
steps: Read the sample bigip.conf and list every virtual server, pool, monitor, persistence profile and iRule.
Read the sample ns.conf and list every lbvserver, servicegroup, monitor and policy binding.
Match objects by intent (VIP address and port) rather than by name.
For each pair, list the fields that must match and the unit conversions needed.
Mark each object type comparable, comparable with mapping, or not comparable.
Write the 'cannot be compared' list with a reason for each entry.
Write the comparison plan: direction, scope, evidence needed, approvers.
Review a partner's checklist and add anything they missed.
success_criteria: Every virtual server on the F5 has a matched target or is listed as unmatched.
Every compared field has a defined unit and default.
The 'cannot be compared' list exists and is justified.
The plan names who approves the result.

common_pitfalls: Matching objects by name; names rarely survive a migration.
Ignoring defaults that are not printed in the configuration.
Treating runtime statistics as configuration differences.
Leaving iRule-to-policy translation to the diff engine instead of human review.

knowledge_check.q: Why is a raw text diff between an F5 and a NetScaler configuration useless?
knowledge_check.a: The dialects describe the same intent with different objects, names, defaults and units [c1][c2].

knowledge_check.q: What is F5's default source-address persistence timeout?
knowledge_check.a: 180 seconds [c18].

knowledge_check.q: What does NetScaler's diff ns config compare?
knowledge_check.a: Two NetScaler configuration files [c2].

knowledge_check.q: What are the three classes in the object checklist?
knowledge_check.a: Comparable, comparable with mapping, not comparable.

modules.title: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP for the workflow
modules.goal: Learners stand up a workbench where Claude can call read-only collector tools through MCP without ever seeing a credential.
learning_objectives: Learners can install Claude Code and write a CLAUDE.md for the comparison repository.
Learners can explain when to use the Agent SDK instead of the interactive CLI.
Learners can build and register an MCP server exposing get_virtual_servers and get_pools.
Learners can keep secrets in environment variables or a vault referenced from .mcp.json.

lessons.title: Claude Code in the repository
points: Create ./CLAUDE.md with /init, then add conventions: canonical model location, never edit fixtures, diff engine must not call a model [c10].
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement; use permission rules or hooks for anything that must be blocked [c10].
Keep it short and import longer standards with @path [c10].
Commit project settings and .mcp.json; keep personal overrides local.

lessons.title: Agent SDK versus CLI
points: CLI for interactive work: writing collectors, reviewing diffs.
Agent SDK for the pipeline: planning and explanation agents run unattended in CI.
Define in-process tools with @tool and create_sdk_mcp_server and list them in allowed_tools as mcp__{server}__{tool} [c12].
Remove built-ins such as Bash and Write from the explanation agent with the tools option [c12].
Use structured output for any result the pipeline consumes [c13].

lessons.title: A read-only collector MCP server
points: Expose get_virtual_servers(device) and get_pools(device), implemented with GET calls only.
Register with claude mcp add --transport stdio collectors -- python servers/collectors.py at project scope so .mcp.json is shared [c11].
Clients discover tools through tools/list and call them through tools/call; return errors with isError [c14].
Return outputSchema-conformant structured results so callers can validate them [c14].

lessons.title: Secrets
points: Reference credentials as ${F5_USER} and ${F5_PASS} in .mcp.json; the values come from the environment or a vault agent [c11].
Tools never echo credentials or auth tokens in results.
Use read-only roles on every device and API.
Check the transcript for secrets as part of the lab sign-off.

instructor_demo: Run /init and edit CLAUDE.md live [c10].
Write the collectors MCP server with two GET-backed tools.
Register it at project scope and show .mcp.json with ${VAR} placeholders [c11].
Ask Claude to list virtual servers on the lab F5 and show the tools/call in the transcript [c14].
Show the same call from an Agent SDK script with allowed_tools limited to the two tools [c12].
Search the transcript for the password and show it is absent.

lab.brief: Stand up the workbench, register the read-only MCP server, and have Claude list the virtual servers on the lab F5 through tool use without ever seeing a password.
steps: Install Claude Code and clone the course repository.
Generate and edit CLAUDE.md with the repository conventions [c10].
Implement get_virtual_servers using GET /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual [c15].
Implement get_pools using GET /mgmt/tm/ltm/pool.
Register the server with claude mcp add at project scope [c11].
Export credentials in your shell only; confirm claude mcp list shows no warnings.
Ask Claude to list the virtual servers and their destinations.
Run the Agent SDK version of the same query and save both transcripts.
success_criteria: Claude lists the lab F5 virtual servers through the MCP tool.
No credential appears in the repository or either transcript.
The server exposes only GET-backed tools.
CLAUDE.md states the 'diff engine never calls a model' rule.

common_pitfalls: Hard-coding credentials in .mcp.json instead of ${VAR} [c11].
Exposing a generic 'run any REST call' tool.
Expecting CLAUDE.md to block actions [c10].
Using an admin role for the collector because it was quicker.

knowledge_check.q: How do you share an MCP server definition with the team?
knowledge_check.a: Add it with --scope project so it is written to .mcp.json in the repository [c11].

knowledge_check.q: When should the pipeline use the Agent SDK rather than the CLI?
knowledge_check.a: For unattended, scripted runs such as CI planning and explanation jobs.

knowledge_check.q: How are SDK tools named in allowed_tools?
knowledge_check.a: mcp__{server}__{tool} [c12].

knowledge_check.q: Which F5 endpoint lists virtual servers?
knowledge_check.a: GET /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual [c15].

modules.title: Collecting configuration from every platform
modules.goal: Learners build idempotent, read-only collectors for F5, NetScaler, Radware Alteon, other load balancers, Cisco APIC and Terraform state that keep the raw payload as evidence.
learning_objectives: Learners can collect F5 configuration with iControl REST and tmsh list output.
Learners can collect NetScaler configuration with NITRO config resources.
Learners can capture Alteon and other load balancer configuration through CLI exports.
Learners can collect APIC objects and Terraform state as JSON.
Learners can enforce the collector contract.

lessons.title: F5 BIG-IP
points: iControl REST: /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual and /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual/~Common~<name>, keyed by name, partition and subPath [c15].
Collect pools, members, monitors, profiles (including persistence) and iRules as separate collections and keep the raw JSON.
tmsh list ltm virtual output is the fallback when REST is unavailable; properties match the ltm virtual man page [c1].
Record partitions; objects outside /Common are often missed.

lessons.title: NetScaler
points: GET /nitro/v1/config/lbvserver with pagesize and pageno for large estates; ?count=yes to check completeness [c16].
Collect servicegroup, monitor, binding and policy resources and keep each response.
Authenticate with the NITRO_AUTH_TOKEN cookie or X-NITRO-USER/X-NITRO-PASS, never both [c16].
Capture show ns runningConfig as a text artifact and compare it with show ns ns.conf to detect unsaved changes [c2].

lessons.title: Radware Alteon and other load balancers
points: Alteon configuration uses menu paths such as /cfg/slb/virt <vsid>/service <vport>; diff flash shows unsaved differences [c23].
Collect a full configuration dump through the CLI and parse it with a deterministic parser per menu path.
For 'Anaya LB', build a CLI capture adapter (fixed command list, prompt detection, timeout) against recorded output.
Without lab appliances, use client-supplied sanitized exports as fixtures.

lessons.title: Cisco APIC and Terraform
points: APIC: POST aaaLogin, then GET /api/mo/uni/tn-<tenant>.json?query-target=subtree for tenant objects; page with page-size [c22].
Terraform: terraform show -json <state or plan file> returns format_version '1.0' and values or resource_changes [c24].
Cloud load balancer resources from state (ALB listeners and target groups [c4], App Gateway components [c5]) become the cloud side of the comparison.
Never run terraform apply from a collector.

lessons.title: Collector contract
points: Read-only: GET and show commands only (APIC login excepted).
Idempotent: two runs produce the same configuration objects.
Timestamped and attributed: device, endpoint, collected_at, collector version.
Raw payload saved under runs/<timestamp>/raw/ and referenced from every normalized field.

instructor_demo: Collect virtual servers from the lab F5 through iControl REST and save the raw JSON [c15].
Collect lbvservers from the NetScaler VPX through NITRO with paging and count [c16].
Show show ns runningConfig versus show ns ns.conf for unsaved changes [c2].
Parse a recorded Alteon /cfg/slb/virt export [c23].
Query an APIC tenant subtree in the DevNet simulator [c22].
Run terraform show -json on the lab state and point out format_version [c24].

lab.brief: Write Python collectors for F5 iControl REST and NetScaler NITRO against the lab devices, then Radware Alteon CLI export and Cisco APIC REST collectors against recorded API fixtures, with Claude drafting the code and you reviewing every diff.
steps: Ask Claude Code to draft the F5 collector; review and correct the diff before accepting.
Run it against the lab F5 and save raw JSON per collection [c15].
Draft and review the NetScaler collector with paging and count checks [c16].
Draft and review the Alteon parser against the recorded export [c23].
Draft and review the APIC collector against recorded responses [c22].
Add a Terraform state reader using terraform show -json [c24].
Run every collector twice and confirm idempotency.
Write unit tests that load each fixture.
success_criteria: Four platform families collected with raw evidence saved.
Each collector is read-only and documented.
Two runs produce identical configuration objects.
You reviewed and can explain every line Claude drafted.

common_pitfalls: Missing objects in non-Common partitions on F5.
Not paging NITRO results and silently truncating large estates [c16].
Comparing running configuration that was never saved [c2].
Letting a collector call terraform apply or plan with write credentials.

knowledge_check.q: How do you check that a NITRO collection is complete?
knowledge_check.a: Compare the collected number with GET ...?count=yes [c16].

knowledge_check.q: Which command renders Terraform state as JSON?
knowledge_check.a: terraform show -json <file> [c24].

knowledge_check.q: Why save raw payloads?
knowledge_check.a: Every normalized field and every diff line must trace back to evidence.

knowledge_check.q: Which Alteon command shows unsaved configuration differences?
knowledge_check.a: diff flash [c23].

modules.title: Normalising into a canonical configuration model
modules.goal: Learners design one canonical Pydantic model with provenance on every field and explicit unknowns, and normalize F5 and NetScaler configurations into it.
learning_objectives: Learners can design canonical classes for VirtualServer, Pool, Member, Monitor, Persistence, SSLProfile and Policy.
Learners can write per-platform mapping tables with unit conversions and defaults.
Learners can attach provenance to every field.
Learners can test round-tripping fixtures through the model.

lessons.title: Designing the canonical model
points: VirtualServer: address, port, protocol, pool ref, persistence ref, ssl refs, policies, vlans or networks, snat mode.
Pool: members, lb method, monitors, priority groups and minimum active members (F5 priority-group 0 to 65535, min-active-members default 0) [c19].
Persistence: type and timeout in seconds; F5 source-addr defaults to 180 s [c18]; NetScaler persistencetype and timeout (default 2) [c16][c17].
Use Pydantic with extra='forbid' so unexpected keys fail loudly instead of being ignored (the default is 'ignore') [c28].
Validate with model_validate() and serialize with model_dump_json() [c28].

lessons.title: Mapping tables and unknowns
points: One table per platform: source field, canonical field, conversion, default if absent.
LB method defaults differ: F5 pools default to round-robin [c19]; NetScaler lbvserver defaults to LEASTCONNECTION [c16]; ALB defaults to round robin [c4].
Unmapped fields go into an unknowns list with the raw value, never dropped.
Profiles with no direct equivalent (for example F5's Fast L4 profile [c20]) are recorded as unknowns for the planner.

lessons.title: Provenance
points: Every field carries source platform, object name, collection time and raw reference (file and JSON pointer).
Defaults applied by the normalizer are marked as 'default', not as observed.
Provenance is what the explanation agent cites later.
Keep the canonical model versioned (for example v1.3) and record the version in every report.

lessons.title: Validation tests
points: Round-trip each fixture: raw to canonical to JSON and back to canonical; objects must be equal.
Test that unknown fields land in unknowns.
Test unit conversion for persistence timeouts and monitor intervals.
Run the tests in CI from day 1.

instructor_demo: Show the canonical model classes and the extra='forbid' setting [c28].
Normalize the lab F5 virtual server with source-addr persistence and show the 180-second default applied with provenance 'default' [c18].
Normalize the NetScaler lbvserver and show persistencetype and timeout mapping [c16].
Show a Fast L4 profile landing in unknowns [c20].
Ask Claude to explain each unknown and show it citing provenance.
Run the round-trip tests.

lab.brief: Build the normaliser for F5 and NetScaler, run both lab configurations through it, and inspect the unknowns list with Claude explaining each one.
steps: Write the canonical Pydantic classes with provenance fields [c28].
Write the F5 mapping table including persistence and pool defaults [c18][c19].
Write the NetScaler mapping table including lbmethod and timeout defaults [c16][c17].
Implement the normalizers and the unknowns collector.
Normalize both lab configurations.
Ask Claude to explain each unknown, citing provenance only.
Write round-trip and conversion tests.
Commit the model with a version number.
success_criteria: Both configurations normalize without validation errors.
Every field has provenance.
Every unmapped field appears in unknowns.
Round-trip tests pass.

common_pitfalls: Using Pydantic's default extra='ignore' and silently losing fields [c28].
Comparing NetScaler timeout values to F5 seconds without confirming units on the appliance.
Recording a normalizer default as if it had been observed on the device.
Changing the canonical model without bumping its version.

knowledge_check.q: What does extra='forbid' do in Pydantic?
knowledge_check.a: Rejects data with keys that do not map to fields [c28].

knowledge_check.q: What is F5's default pool load balancing method?
knowledge_check.a: Round-robin [c19].

knowledge_check.q: What is NetScaler's default lbmethod for an lbvserver?
knowledge_check.a: LEASTCONNECTION [c16].

knowledge_check.q: What four facts make up provenance?
knowledge_check.a: Source platform, object name, collection time, raw reference.

modules.title: Migration planning with Claude
modules.goal: Learners build a planning agent that turns a source inventory and target capabilities into a structured migration plan that cites the inventory and states what cannot be mapped.
learning_objectives: Learners can prompt Claude with inventory and target capabilities to produce a JSON plan.
Learners can require mapping, gap, dependency order, risk, confidence, owner and citation fields.
Learners can test the planner with incomplete and contradictory inventories.
Learners can review and version plans in Git.

lessons.title: Inputs to the planner
points: The canonical inventory and unknowns from module 4.
A target capability sheet: for NetScaler, persistence types and backup virtual servers [c16][c17]; responder policies for redirects [c21]; for cloud targets, ALB and App Gateway components [c4][c5].
Vendor migration tools as reference points: F5 ACC to AS3 [c6], F5 Journeys for UCS-based migrations and parity gaps [c7], NetScaler Configuration Builder and its known blind spots [c3].
Claude reads these through tools, not pasted whole configurations.

lessons.title: The plan schema
points: Each step: source object id, target object type, mapping, feature gap, dependency order, risk, confidence, owner, citations to inventory ids.
Return the plan as structured output validated against the schema [c13].
Dependency order follows object dependencies: monitors, then pools or service groups, then virtual servers.
Gaps example: an iRule redirect maps to a responder action and policy bound to the lbvserver, reviewed by a person [c21].

lessons.title: Handling bad inventories
points: Missing values (for example no persistence timeout recorded) must appear as unknown, not as an assumed default.
Contradictions (two virtual servers claiming the same address and port) must be flagged and left unmapped.
Priority groups on F5 pools [c19] need a design decision on the target, such as a backup virtual server on NetScaler [c17]; the planner proposes, a person decides.
Named expressions and responder HTML pages are not detected by NetScaler's Configuration Builder [c3]; the plan must list them as manual items.

lessons.title: Review and versioning
points: Plans are committed to Git as JSON plus a rendered summary.
A pull request is the first human checkpoint; reviewers comment on steps, not formatting.
Plan versions are referenced by the later diff and approval package.
Reject plans whose citations do not resolve to inventory ids before the review starts.

instructor_demo: Show the inventory, unknowns and capability sheet the planner receives.
Run the planner and show the structured plan with citations [c13].
Show an iRule-to-responder mapping marked for human review [c21].
Feed a contradictory inventory and show the conflict flagged.
Open a pull request with the plan.

lab.brief: Generate a physical-to-cloud plan for the lab inventory, then feed Claude a deliberately contradictory inventory and verify it flags the conflict instead of inventing a mapping.
steps: Write the PlanStep and Plan Pydantic models.
Write the capability sheet for the cloud NetScaler target [c16][c17][c21].
Write the planner prompt with citation and unknowns rules.
Run the planner with output_format [c13].
Validate every citation against the inventory.
Run the contradictory inventory and check for a flagged conflict.
Run an inventory with a missing persistence timeout and check it is unknown.
Commit the plan and open a pull request.
success_criteria: The plan validates and every step cites inventory ids.
Gaps and manual items are listed explicitly.
The contradictory inventory produces a flagged conflict, not a mapping.
The plan is under review in a pull request.

common_pitfalls: Pasting whole configurations into the prompt instead of tool access.
Accepting high confidence on steps that map logic (iRules) automatically.
Forgetting manual items the vendor tool cannot detect [c3].
Plans not versioned and not tied to a collection run.

knowledge_check.q: What must the planner do with a value missing from the inventory?
knowledge_check.a: Mark it unknown, never assume a default.

knowledge_check.q: What does F5 ACC convert configuration into?
knowledge_check.a: AS3 or Declarative Onboarding declarations [c6].

knowledge_check.q: Which NetScaler items does Configuration Builder not detect?
knowledge_check.a: Named expressions and responder HTML pages [c3].

knowledge_check.q: Which NetScaler feature replaces a simple redirect iRule?
knowledge_check.a: A responder action and policy bound to the virtual server [c21].

slides_and_assets: Target capability sheets (NetScaler, ALB, App Gateway).
Slide: vendor migration tools and their limits.

modules.title: The deterministic diff engine
modules.goal: Learners implement a Python diff engine that compares canonical models field by field, classifies differences by severity and produces a JSON report without ever calling a model.
learning_objectives: Learners can implement field-by-field comparison with ordering and set semantics.
Learners can define severity rules and exemptions.
Learners can produce a machine-readable report and a human summary.
Learners can prove with tests that seeded mismatches are always caught.

lessons.title: Comparison semantics
points: Match objects by intent key (address, port, protocol) produced in module 4.
Compare lists as sets where order does not matter (pool members) and as sequences where it does (policy rule order).
Compare normalized values only, after unit conversion, with defaults marked.
Tolerances are explicit, versioned rules, not ad hoc code.

lessons.title: Severity classification
points: Blocking: changes traffic behavior at cut-over (persistence type or timeout, pool membership, VIP port, certificate).
Warning: likely behavior change under load or failure (monitor interval, priority groups versus backup design) [c19].
Informational: cosmetic or platform-inherent (object names, descriptions).
Exemptions are listed per platform pair with a reason, for example backend HTTP/1.1 on App Gateway [c5].

lessons.title: The report
points: JSON: run id, model version, source and target, per-object diffs with field, source value, target value, severity, provenance refs.
Human summary: counts per severity and the blocking list.
The engine never calls a model; Claude reads the report later through tools.
Report schema is versioned and validated with Pydantic [c28].

lessons.title: Testing
points: pytest suites with fixtures for matched, mismatched and missing objects.
Seeded mismatch: source-addr persistence 300 s on the source versus 180 s on the target must be blocking.
Property-style tests: shuffling member order never creates a difference.
Tests run on every pull request.

instructor_demo: Walk through the engine's comparison of two VirtualServer objects.
Show the severity rules file.
Seed a persistence timeout mismatch into the target and run the engine.
Show the JSON report line and the summary.
Run the pytest suite and show the seeded test.

lab.brief: Implement the diff engine, seed a hidden persistence timeout mismatch into the target configuration, and prove the test suite catches it.
steps: Implement match_objects() by intent key.
Implement compare_fields() with set and sequence semantics.
Write the severity rules file and loader.
Implement report generation validated by a Pydantic schema [c28].
Write fixtures and tests for matched, mismatched and missing cases.
Seed the persistence timeout mismatch in a hidden fixture.
Run the suite and confirm the seeded test fails before the rule exists and passes after.
Commit through a pull request.
success_criteria: The engine produces a valid JSON report.
The seeded mismatch is reported as blocking.
Shuffled member order produces no difference.
No model call exists anywhere in the engine code.

common_pitfalls: Comparing unnormalized values.
Severity decided in code branches instead of a rules file.
Treating platform defaults as differences when both sides are equivalent after normalization.
Letting the engine call Claude 'just to summarize'.

knowledge_check.q: Why does the diff engine never call a model?
knowledge_check.a: So the diff is deterministic, repeatable and testable; Claude only explains it.

knowledge_check.q: Give one blocking and one informational difference.
knowledge_check.a: Blocking: persistence timeout or pool membership. Informational: object name.

knowledge_check.q: How do you prove the engine catches a mismatch?
knowledge_check.a: A seeded mismatch fixture with a test that must fail if it is missed.

knowledge_check.q: Why compare pool members as a set?
knowledge_check.a: Member order does not change behavior, so order differences are not real differences.

modules.title: Claude explains the differences
modules.goal: Learners build an explanation agent that reads the diff report through tools and writes explanations, drift summaries and remediation steps with every claim tied to a report line.
learning_objectives: Learners can expose get_diff and get_object tools to Claude.
Learners can require structured explanations with citations to report lines.
Learners can produce two audiences' outputs from one report.
Learners can reject any output that references objects not in the report.

lessons.title: Tool access, not pasting
points: Define get_diff(run_id, severity) and get_object(run_id, object_id) tools with input schemas [c8][c12].
Claude responds with tool_use, your code returns tool_result [c8].
Use strict: true on custom tool definitions when calling the API directly so calls match the schema [c8].
Remove file and shell built-ins from the explanation agent [c12].

lessons.title: Structured explanation output
points: Per difference: what differs, why it matters for traffic, recommended remediation, confidence, citation to the report line.
Example: source-address persistence shorter on the target means sessions may move to another server after the shorter idle time; remediation sets the target timeout to match.
Use output_format with a Pydantic schema [c13].
Unknown impacts are stated as unknown.

lessons.title: Two audiences
points: Operations managers: drift summary with counts, blocking items and cut-over risk.
Engineers: remediation steps with target CLI or API objects named, never executed.
Both are generated from the same report and cite the same lines.
Use the same schema with an audience field so tests can check that both outputs cover the same blocking items [c13].

lessons.title: Guarding against hallucinated objects
points: A deterministic check confirms every object id and report line referenced exists.
Outputs that fail the check are rejected and regenerated once, then escalated.
Tool annotations are not trusted for safety; tools themselves are read-only [c14].
Log rejected outputs with the reason so prompt changes can be evaluated against them.

instructor_demo: Show the get_diff and get_object tool definitions [c12].
Run the explanation agent on the seeded mismatch and show the tool calls [c8].
Show the structured explanation with citation diff#L3 style references [c13].
Inject a fake object id into the output and show the check rejecting it.
Generate the manager summary and engineer remediation from the same report.

lab.brief: Build the explanation agent with the Agent SDK, run it on the day's diff report, and verify every statement traces to a report line.
steps: Implement get_diff and get_object as SDK tools [c12].
Write the Explanation Pydantic schema with citations [c13].
Write the prompt for engineers and the prompt for managers.
Run on the module 6 report.
Implement the citation and object existence check.
Test the check with a deliberately bad output.
Render the remediation report template.
Commit outputs with the run id.
success_criteria: Every explanation cites a report line that exists.
No output references an object outside the report.
Manager and engineer outputs agree on blocking items.
Remediation steps are proposals only; nothing is executed.

common_pitfalls: Pasting the full report into the prompt and losing traceability.
Allowing the agent to propose remediation it then executes.
Accepting plausible explanations without the existence check.
Different counts in manager and engineer outputs.

knowledge_check.q: What stop_reason indicates Claude wants to call your tool?
knowledge_check.a: tool_use [c8].

knowledge_check.q: What does strict: true do on a tool definition?
knowledge_check.a: Ensures tool calls always match the schema [c8].

knowledge_check.q: How do you catch a hallucinated object?
knowledge_check.a: A deterministic check that every referenced id exists in the report.

knowledge_check.q: Why give Claude tools instead of the whole report?
knowledge_check.a: Smaller context, targeted reads and citations that map to specific lines.

modules.title: Guardrails, approvals and audit for configuration comparison
modules.goal: Learners wire the pipeline so that every comparison becomes a reviewed pull request and a ServiceNow change routed for approval, with no write capability exposed to Claude and a full audit log.
learning_objectives: Learners can verify that all collectors use read-only credentials and no MCP tool can write.
Learners can create a ServiceNow change through the Table API and attach the report.
Learners can publish a comparison as a GitHub pull request with protection rules.
Learners can keep an audit log of prompts, tool calls, outputs and human decisions.

lessons.title: No write path for Claude
points: List every MCP tool and confirm each is GET or show only [c14].
Deny rules and the tools option keep shell and file writes away from pipeline agents [c12].
Remediation is a document, applied by a person through normal change control.
MCP guidance: human in the loop and confirmation for sensitive operations [c14].

lessons.title: ServiceNow change record
points: Create a change with POST /api/now/table/change_request; POST inserts one record at a time [c27].
Store the run id, report summary and pull request link in the change description; attach the report.
A record-based Flow Designer trigger on the new change routes it for approval to the named approver; expect queue delay [c31].
Read state back with GET on the change before allowing any remediation step [c27].

lessons.title: GitHub pull request
points: Each comparison run opens a pull request containing the plan, report, explanation and evidence index.
Protect main: required approving reviews (optionally from code owners), required status checks, stale approvals dismissed on new commits [c26].
Reviewers approve the comparison, not the remediation.
The pull request and change cross-link.

lessons.title: Audit log
points: Log prompts, tool calls with inputs, tool outputs (hashed), model outputs and human decisions with timestamps.
MCP clients should log tool usage for audit [c14].
Store the audit log with the raw evidence, outside the agent's write scope.
A blocked remediation attempt is logged with who, what and why.

instructor_demo: List MCP tools and show none can write [c14].
Create a change through the Table API and show it in the PDI [c27].
Show the Flow Designer approval routing firing [c31].
Open the pull request and show branch protection blocking merge without approval [c26].
Attempt an unapproved remediation and show the block and audit entry.

lab.brief: Wire the pipeline to create a ServiceNow change via the Table API and a GitHub pull request, then attempt an unapproved remediation and confirm it is blocked and logged.
steps: Audit your MCP tool list for write capability.
Implement create_change() with POST on change_request [c27].
Build the Flow Designer flow that routes the change to the approver [c31].
Implement open_pr() with the plan, report, explanation and evidence index.
Enable branch protection with required reviews and checks [c26].
Implement the remediation gate that checks change approval state through GET [c27].
Attempt remediation before approval and capture the block.
Review the audit log for the full run.
success_criteria: A change record exists, linked to the pull request.
The pull request cannot merge without review and green checks.
The unapproved remediation is blocked and logged.
The audit log covers every prompt, tool call and decision.

common_pitfalls: Giving the pipeline service account write roles on devices 'for later'.
Approving in GitHub and assuming the change is approved too.
Not handling Flow Designer delay before checking approval [c31].
Audit logs that the agent can modify.

knowledge_check.q: Which Table API call creates a change request?
knowledge_check.a: POST /api/now/table/change_request [c27].

knowledge_check.q: Which branch protection setting forces re-approval after new commits?
knowledge_check.a: Dismissing stale approvals when new commits are pushed [c26].

knowledge_check.q: What does the pipeline do before any remediation step?
knowledge_check.a: Reads the change record and requires an approved state.

knowledge_check.q: Why is remediation a document rather than an action?
knowledge_check.a: Claude has no write path; people apply changes through change control.

modules.title: Scheduling, Terraform plan checks and GitHub Actions
modules.goal: Learners run comparisons on a schedule and on Terraform pull requests, comparing the Terraform plan with live collected state and publishing results to the pull request and ServiceNow.
learning_objectives: Learners can schedule comparisons with GitHub Actions cron.
Learners can run terraform plan in CI and read its JSON output.
Learners can compare planned cloud load balancer changes with live collected state.
Learners can publish results and operate the pipeline with a runbook.

lessons.title: Scheduling
points: on: schedule with POSIX cron runs in UTC by default on the latest commit of the default branch; minimum interval 5 minutes [c25].
Combine schedules and read github.event.schedule to vary behavior [c25].
Also trigger on pull_request for paths that change Terraform code.
Scheduled runs are read-only and post results; they never remediate.

lessons.title: Terraform plan in CI
points: terraform plan -out=tfplan -detailed-exitcode: exit 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes present [c9].
terraform show -json tfplan gives resource_changes with change.actions and before and after values [c24].
resource_drift lists changes Terraform detected outside its control [c24].
A -refresh-only plan shows state drift without proposing configuration changes [c9].

lessons.title: Plan versus live state
points: Normalize the planned after-values for the cloud load balancer into the canonical model.
Compare with the live collected state; differences on both sides are drift.
Flag planned replacements (['delete','create']) on listeners or target groups as blocking for review [c24].
Feed results to the explanation agent like any other report.

lessons.title: Publishing and operations
points: Comment the summary on the pull request and update the ServiceNow change [c27].
Archive reports and evidence per run.
Runbook: collector failures, token expiry, retries with backoff, fixture refresh.
Alert on scheduled run failures, not only on differences.

instructor_demo: Show the workflow file with schedule and pull_request triggers [c25].
Run terraform plan with -detailed-exitcode and show exit code 2 [c9].
Show terraform show -json output and a resource_changes entry [c24].
Compare the plan with live ALB or App Gateway state and show a drift line.
Show the pull request comment and the ServiceNow update [c27].

lab.brief: Build the GitHub Actions workflow that runs the comparison, compares a Terraform plan against the live cloud load balancer, and comments the result on the pull request.
steps: Write the workflow with schedule and pull_request triggers [c25].
Add terraform init and plan with -out and -detailed-exitcode [c9].
Convert the plan with terraform show -json [c24].
Normalize planned values and run the diff against live state.
Run the explanation agent on the result.
Comment the summary on the pull request.
Update the ServiceNow change with the result [c27].
Write the runbook.
success_criteria: The workflow runs on schedule and on Terraform pull requests.
Planned replacements are flagged blocking.
Drift between plan and live state is reported with provenance.
Results appear on the pull request and the change record.

common_pitfalls: Treating exit code 2 from -detailed-exitcode as a failure [c9].
Expecting cron to run exactly on time and in local time zone [c25].
Running terraform apply from the comparison workflow.
No alert when the scheduled run itself fails.

knowledge_check.q: What does terraform plan -detailed-exitcode return when changes are present?
In what time zone do scheduled workflows run by default?
knowledge_check.a: UTC [c25].

knowledge_check.q: How does Terraform JSON represent a replacement?
knowledge_check.a: change.actions of ['delete','create'] or ['create','delete'] [c24].

knowledge_check.q: What is the shortest schedule interval in GitHub Actions?
knowledge_check.a: Once every 5 minutes [c25].

lessons.title: Run the pipeline
points: Collect from the lab F5 [c15] and cloud NetScaler [c16].

Seed one surprise mismatch chosen by the instructor.
Teams may not edit fixtures or severity rules after the surprise mismatch is seeded.

lessons.title: The approval package
points: Plan, severity report, Claude explanation, evidence index, unknowns and manual items.
ServiceNow change created via the Table API [c27].
Pull request under branch protection [c26].
Unknowns and manual items (for example iRule logic and named expressions [c3]) are listed with owners.

lessons.title: Acceptance review
points: Check every module 1 checklist row.
Confirm no change was applied and the attempt log is clean.
Limitations statement and next steps.
Reviewers replay one diff line from report to raw evidence to show traceability.

instructor_demo: Seed the surprise mismatch in the target.
Show the acceptance checklist and scoring rubric.
Model a two-minute acceptance walkthrough.
Show how the audit log will be checked.

lab.brief: Run the full pipeline on the lab physical F5 and cloud NetScaler, produce the approval package with ServiceNow change and pull request, and present it for acceptance review against the module one checklist.
steps: Run collectors on both platforms.

capstone_plan.brief: Teams run the complete pipeline on the lab physical F5 and cloud NetScaler: collect, normalize, plan, diff and explain, then deliver an approval package with a ServiceNow change and a GitHub pull request, with no change applied and a full audit trail.

Explanations and remediation proposals validated against the report.

promo_video_research.hook_basis: A cut-over on a fixed date with a target configuration rebuilt by hand from a spreadsheet is a teaching scenario, but the underlying risk is real: vendor tools compare or migrate within one ecosystem [c2][c3][c6][c7], and defaults differ across platforms, for example F5's 180-second source-address persistence [c18] versus NetScaler's lbvserver persistence timeout default of 2 [c16].

claims_check.basis: Taken directly from the client input (cloud-cloud, physical to cloud, cloud to physical).

Course design: F5 iControl REST, NetScaler NITRO, Radware Alteon, Cisco APIC and Terraform state [c15][c16][c22][c23][c24]. Alteon is CLI-export based in the lab, so 'API family' is loose wording for Radware.
Design goal enforced by read-only tools, branch protection and change approval [c14][c26][c27]; a property of the course build.
Real endpoint families [c15][c16]; counts are illustrative.

claims_check.claim: '6 unknowns (f5 fastL4 profile: no NITRO equivalent)'
claims_check.basis: Fast L4 is a real F5 profile [c20]. That it has 'no NITRO equivalent' is a simplification for the lab narrative (NetScaler has its own TCP profiles); present it as an unmapped field requiring review, not as a vendor fact.

claims_check.claim: 'gap: F5 iRule redirect_legacy has no NITRO equivalent -> responder policy'
claims_check.basis: Responder policies handle redirects on NetScaler [c21]; the specific iRule is a teaching scenario.

claims_check.claim: 'risk: 2 pools use priority groups; NetScaler backup vserver proposed'
claims_check.basis: F5 priority groups [c19] and NetScaler backup virtual servers [c17] both exist; the mapping is a design choice, not a one-to-one equivalent.

claims_check.claim: 'unknown: persistence timeout on vs_app_api (not in inventory)'
claims_check.basis: Teaching scenario showing the planner must mark missing data unknown.
Illustrative output of the course plan schema; values invented.

claims_check.claim: Diff line: 'vs_app_api persistence: source_ip 180s BLOCKING / source value 300s' and 'session drops likely after 180s idle; set timeout 300'
claims_check.basis: Teaching scenario. 180 s matches F5's source-addr default [c18]; on the NetScaler target the equivalent setting is the lbvserver timeout (default 2) [c16][c17], so the lab should show the value after unit normalization. Wording 'session drops' should be read as 'persistence lost', not dropped connections.
Teaching scenario; interval values are illustrative and show a warning-class difference.

claims_check.claim: 'servicenow: CHG0041877 created via Table API approver: netops-lead'
claims_check.basis: Change records are created with POST on the Table API [c27] and routed by Flow Designer [c31]; number invented.

claims_check.claim: 'github: PR #58 opened checks: diff-engine passed, drift-check passed'
claims_check.basis: Status checks and required reviews via branch protection [c26]; illustrative.

claims_check.claim: Terraform plan output compared against live state before apply
claims_check.basis: terraform plan and its JSON output support this [c9][c24].

citations.title: ltm virtual - F5 TMSH Reference v17
citations.key_fact: A BIG-IP virtual server is defined by properties such as destination (default any:any), pool, profiles, persist, rules (iRules), policies, vlans and source-address-translation; the snat and snatpool attributes are deprecated in favor of source-address-translation; show virtual displays statistics and status.

citations.title: System base operations
citations.key_fact: NetScaler configuration is stored in /nsconfig/ns.conf and must be saved with save ns config to survive restarts; show ns runningConfig and show ns ns.conf display running and saved configuration; diff ns config <configfile> <configfile2> (GUI: System > Diagnostics > Configuration difference) compares two configuration files.

citations.title: Migrate NetScaler application configuration using StyleBooks Configuration Builder
citations.key_fact: The Configuration Builder takes a NetScaler instance, pasted ns.conf or application CLI commands, or an uploaded file, produces a StyleBook and config pack for duplicating configuration to other instances, reports missed or unsupported configuration to apply separately, and does not identify named expressions and responder HTML pages, which must be configured on the target before migration.

citations.title: What is an Application Load Balancer?
citations.key_fact: An ALB has listeners (protocol and port), rules (priority, conditions, actions) with a mandatory default rule per listener, and target groups with per-target-group health checks; a target can be registered with multiple target groups; the default routing algorithm is round robin, with least outstanding requests as an alternative.

citations.title: Application gateway components
citations.key_fact: Azure Application Gateway uses frontend IPs, listeners (multi-site listeners support wildcards and up to five host names), request routing rules (basic, advanced or path-based; one listener per rule), backend settings, backend pools and health probes; HTTP/2 applies to client connections only and backend communication is always HTTP/1.1.

citations.title: F5 BIG-IP Automation Config Converter (BIG-IP ACC)
citations.key_fact: BIG-IP ACC (1.24) converts BIG-IP configuration files into AS3 or Declarative Onboarding declarations based on supported classes; it is a community-supported offering with source code and issues on GitHub.

citations.title: Welcome to the F5 BIG-IP Migration Assistant - Now the F5 Journeys App
citations.key_fact: The BIG-IP Migration Assistant is deprecated and replaced by F5 Journeys (github.com/f5devcentral/f5-journeys), which loads UCS or UCS plus AS3 sources, migrates from any version starting at 11.5.0 to a higher one including VELOS and rSeries, flags feature-parity gaps with built-in fixes, and can migrate applications to AS3.

citations.title: Tool use with Claude
citations.key_fact: To have Claude call a function you define, pass a tool with an input_schema; Claude responds with stop_reason tool_use and tool_use blocks, your code runs the operation and returns a tool_result; adding strict: true to a custom tool definition ensures Claude's tool calls always match the schema.

citations.title: terraform plan command reference
citations.supports: Scheduling, Terraform plan checks and GitHub Actions
citations.key_fact: terraform plan compares configuration with prior state and shows + create, - destroy, ~ update in-place and -/+ replace; -detailed-exitcode returns 0 (no changes), 1 (error) or 2 (changes present); -out=FILE saves a plan for later apply, otherwise the plan is speculative; -refresh-only creates a plan that only updates state to match changes made outside Terraform.

citations.title: How Claude remembers your project
citations.supports: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP
citations.key_fact: Project instructions live in ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md and are shared via version control; /init generates a starting file; @path imports pull in other files; CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, so blocking actions requires a PreToolUse hook; files should stay under about 200 lines.

citations.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP
citations.supports: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP
citations.key_fact: claude mcp add registers HTTP (recommended for remote) or stdio servers (arguments after -- go to the process); SSE is deprecated; scopes are local (default), project (.mcp.json, shared via Git) and user; .mcp.json expands ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} so credentials stay in the environment.

citations.title: Give Claude custom tools (Agent SDK)
citations.supports: Setting up the Agent SDK; Claude explains the differences
citations.key_fact: Python tools are defined with @tool and wrapped with create_sdk_mcp_server, passed via ClaudeAgentOptions(mcp_servers=...), and named mcp__{server}__{tool} in allowed_tools; the tools option removes built-ins from Claude's context; handlers return content and may set is_error; readOnlyHint is metadata, not enforcement.

citations.title: Get structured output from agents
citations.supports: Migration planning with Claude; Claude explains the differences
citations.key_fact: output_format={'type': 'json_schema', 'schema': ...} returns validated JSON in ResultMessage.structured_output; Pydantic's model_json_schema() can supply the schema; validation uses JSON Schema draft-07 with re-prompting, and failure yields subtype error_max_structured_output_retries.

citations.title: Tools (MCP specification 2025-06-18)
citations.key_fact: MCP tools are listed with tools/list and invoked with tools/call; definitions include inputSchema and optional outputSchema and annotations; results can carry structuredContent and isError; there should always be a human in the loop able to deny invocations, annotations are untrusted unless from trusted servers, and clients should log tool usage for audit.

citations.title: APIRef_tm_ltm_virtual (iControl REST)
citations.key_fact: The iControl REST collection URI for virtual servers is /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual (OPTIONS, GET) and the resource URI is /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual/~resource id (OPTIONS, GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, POST), with natural key name, partition and subPath.

citations.title: lbvserver configuration (NITRO API 13.1)
citations.key_fact: GET /nitro/v1/config/lbvserver lists virtual servers (with attrs, filter, view=summary and pagesize/pageno), /nitro/v1/config/lbvserver/<name> returns one and ?count=yes returns a count; requests use Cookie NITRO_AUTH_TOKEN or X-NITRO-USER/X-NITRO-PASS; fields include persistencetype (SOURCEIP, COOKIEINSERT, SSLSESSION, RULE, NONE and others), timeout (default 2, range 0 to 1440), lbmethod (default LEASTCONNECTION), and read-only curstate and effectivestate.

citations.title: lb vserver - ADC CLI Commands
citations.key_fact: In the CLI reference, timeout is the time period for which a persistence session is in effect (default 2, maximum 1440); persistenceBackup and backupPersistenceTimeout provide backup persistence; -backupVServer names a backup virtual server; show lb vserver displays statistics for a virtual server.

citations.title: ltm persistence source-addr - F5 TMSH Reference
citations.key_fact: The source-addr persistence profile timeout defaults to 180 seconds; mask defaults to ::; match-across-pools, match-across-services and match-across-virtuals default to disabled.

citations.title: ltm pool - F5 TMSH Reference
citations.key_fact: Pools default to round-robin load balancing; members can be placed in priority-group 0 to 65535 with traffic sent to groups in priority order; min-active-members (default 0) controls priority-based activation; member ratio defaults to 1; member monitor defaults to the pool's monitors.

citations.title: ltm profile fastl4 - F5 TMSH Reference
citations.key_fact: The Fast L4 profile is the default profile the system uses for a basic configuration of non-UDP traffic, with options such as idle-timeout; changes to an active Fast L4 profile take effect for new connections after the idle-timeout passes.

citations.title: Responder
citations.key_fact: A NetScaler responder action can generate a custom response, redirect a request or reset a connection; a responder policy selects the traffic and is bound to a bind point such as a load balancing virtual server; responder works on client-side parameters, unlike rewrite.

citations.title: Cisco APIC REST API Configuration Guide - Using the REST API
citations.key_fact: APIC objects are read at /api/mo/{dn}.{json|xml} and classes at /api/class/{className}; aaaLogin returns a token used as APIC-cookie (default session timeout 600 s); query-target takes self, children or subtree; query-target-filter supports operators such as eq and wcard; page and page-size paginate; GET makes no changes.

citations.title: Alteon 31.0.11.0 Release Notes - Maintenance fixes
citations.key_fact: Radware's fix list references Alteon CLI paths such as /cfg/slb/virt <vsid>/service <vport> for virtual service configuration, the diff flash command that shows pending versus saved configuration, and /stats/slb/virt and /stats/slb/group for statistics.

citations.title: JSON Output Format
citations.supports: Collecting configuration (Terraform state); Scheduling, Terraform plan checks and GitHub Actions
citations.key_fact: terraform show -json <FILE> renders a plan or state file as JSON with a format_version key ('1.0' as of Terraform 1.1.0); plans contain resource_changes (each with address and change.actions such as ['no-op'], ['create'], ['update'], ['delete','create'] or ['delete'], plus before and after values) and resource_drift for changes detected outside Terraform.

citations.title: Events that trigger workflows
citations.supports: Scheduling, Terraform plan checks and GitHub Actions
citations.key_fact: The schedule event uses POSIX cron syntax, runs in UTC by default (an IANA timezone can be set), runs on the latest commit on the default branch, and the shortest interval is once every 5 minutes; multiple schedules can be combined and the triggering one read from github.event.schedule.

citations.title: About protected branches
citations.key_fact: Branch protection rules can require pull request reviews before merging (a set number of approving reviews, optionally from code owners), require status checks, and dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed; by default force pushes and deletions are blocked on protected branches.

citations.title: Table API
citations.key_fact: POST /api/now/table/{tableName} inserts one record (no bulk insert) and PATCH/PUT /api/now/table/{tableName}/{sys_id} update a record; GET supports sysparm_query, sysparm_fields, sysparm_limit (default 10000), sysparm_offset and sysparm_display_value.

citations.title: Models (Pydantic)
citations.supports: Normalising into a canonical configuration model
citations.key_fact: Pydantic models validate input on instantiation or with model_validate() and model_validate_json(), raising ValidationError when data cannot be parsed; model_dump() and model_dump_json() serialize; the extra setting is 'ignore' by default, 'forbid' rejects unknown keys and 'allow' keeps them in __pydantic_extra__.

citations.title: Try BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Virtual Editions
citations.key_fact: F5 offers a 30-day free trial of BIG-IP Virtual Edition requested through MyF5 (My Products & Plans > Trials > BIG-IP Virtual Edition & BIG-IQ Virtual Edition).

citations.title: Licensing (NetScaler VPX Express)
citations.key_fact: NetScaler VPX Express for on-premises and cloud deployments needs no license file and offers 20 Mbps bandwidth, up to 250 SSL sessions and 20 Mbps SSL throughput; from 14.1 build 29.65 it includes the advanced Premium features.

citations.title: Architecture Overview (Flow Designer / Workflow Studio)
citations.key_fact: Flows start from record-based, schedule-based or application-based triggers; queued events are processed in the order added, so a flow may start with a delay; process plans are compiled just in time and cached when unchanged.
